# Sprinting — Class 6 of 12

**Primary effort:** Organize the first forward push and the next support exchange while controlling the body line. Combine short start practice with gym support for upright foot return and rapid hip/ankle force.

**Baseline and review:** Ages 12–14 with established basic lifting/landing technique, under qualified coaching. Reviewed Classes 1–5, strength anchors, workload/drill history including replacements, audits, equipment assumptions and feedback. **Actual attendance, execution, loads and recovery remain unknown.** This class consolidates related demands through distinct task variants; no improvement or earned intensity increase is assumed. Strength doses remain at Class 5 levels.

**Framework:** `Sprinting > Acceleration (straight-line and multidirectional)` and `Sprinting > Maximum velocity`. The start application is straight-line; upright work is supplemental gym practice. No actual maximum-velocity running is possible in this prescription, and stationary placement cues are not literal full-speed touchdown geometry.

**Quality marker within E1:** Record first stepping foot, whether the lean stays organized, whether the first recovery step catches/supports the moving body without a long reach or waist fold, attempted/controlled starts and stopping control. Observe only the four prescribed attempts. Falling starts are a new protocol, not directly comparable to standing, half-kneeling or three-point start scores.

## 1. Access & Prepare 1

Complete the **existing predetermined Access & Prepare 1**, unchanged and supplied separately. Its content, duration and workload remain unknown here. Use actual preparation/readiness to qualify the listed work; no new preparation sequence is authored.

## 2. Explosiveness — Exactly 6 Exercises

E1 is the main performance task. Work in order; quick clean intent and full recovery take priority over distance, height or cadence. The upright drill has a smaller dose because starts return today.

| # | Exercise | Sets × reps | Specific job in this workout |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Falling Start — first two steps** | **2 × 2 starts**, one with each first stepping foot per pair. At most **2 driving foot strikes or 3 m**, whichever comes first; then progressively slow and stop by **9 m**. **75 s between starts; 120 s between pairs.** | **Main task:** turn a controlled forward whole-body lean into the first supporting push and next step. Start with feet parallel near hip width, arms relaxed; let the body tip forward from the ankles without folding at the waist. Initiate the selected stepping foot early enough to stay in control; do not wait for a near-fall or chase a maximum lean. First pair is controlled fast to establish stopping; second pair uses the fastest clean intent that preserves it. No jump into the start. |
| 2 | **Staggered-Stance Broad Jump to Parallel Two-Foot Stick** | **1 × 2 per starting front leg**, bodyweight, natural arms. **20 s between same-front-leg reps; 45 s between sides.** | Coordinate a forward impulse from both legs in an offset base, complementing the start's first-step push. Set feet about hip width apart with a small fore-aft offset; use one controlled dip, push through both feet and jump forward a modest distance. Bring feet approximately parallel for a **2 s held landing**. Do not turn it into a one-leg bound or a split-stance receiver. Reduce offset/distance for twisting or a visibly one-sided push. |
| 3 | **Wall-Lean Single-Leg Pogo** | **1 × 2 low hops per support leg**, bodyweight; **60 s between legs**. Keep the free thigh comfortably raised and still; controlled two-foot reset after the final same-leg landing. | Express brief ankle recoil while preserving a forward body line against firm hand support. Use both palms on an immovable non-slip wall near shoulder height and a comfortable shallow whole-body lean. Make very small same-leg hops in place; support knee stays soft, hands remain fixed and free leg does not pulse or exchange. Reduce lean/amplitude for hand/foot slip, pelvic sag or drifting contacts. This requires a verified wall; use the stated replacement if unavailable. |
| 4 | **Split Jump — single scissor exchange to stick** | **1 × 2 per starting front leg**, bodyweight, modest height. **20 s between same-start reps; 45 s between starting sides.** | Coordinate rapid opposing thigh movement with a new support configuration. From a comfortable split stance, dip slightly, jump upward and exchange the feet once in the air; land with the opposite foot forward and hold **2 s**. Reset to the named starting stance before the next rep. Feet stay on separate hip-width tracks, not a tightrope; no repeated bouncing or second exchange. Lower height/range for rotation, crossed feet or an unstable receiver. |
| 5 | **Stationary Single-Leg Step-Over Run** | **1 × 2 cycles per target leg**, bodyweight; **75 s between target legs**. One target-foot contact + one low opposite-foot contact = one cycle: **8 total running contacts**, 4/foot. | Bring the controlled lower-leg release from earlier skipping into an asymmetric running exchange. Recover the target heel beneath the hip, lift that thigh comfortably, let its lower leg open modestly, then return the foot near its normal standing position as the opposite leg uses a low running step. Use small flight and natural arms; no kick, backward claw or literal obstacle to clear. Lower the release range/cadence for reaching, leaning or extra hops. Finish after the second cycle. |
| 6 | **Dead-Stop Kettlebell Swing — two hands, one float per reset** | **2 × 3 singles**; **20 s after each parked rep within a set, 90 s between sets**. Choose a light-to-moderate bell that permits a crisp hip drive and controlled park; no effort to grind or reach a fixed height. | Re-establish hip loading and a rapid drive for each initiation rather than relying on a continuous swing rhythm. With the bell parked just ahead within comfortable reach, hinge with a stable spine, grip with both hands, hike it back once, drive the hips to a tall finish and let the bell float **no higher than chest level**. Guide its return through the hinge and park it under control before resetting. Feet remain planted; no arm lift, backward lean or release. Reduce bell size/load for a slow drive or unstable hike/park. This is a parked-single variant of the earlier swing family, not a swing without any backswing. |

**Recovery:** **90 s after E1–E4; 60 s after E5–E6**, including the transition to S1. Setup/instruction may occupy recovery; count actual elapsed time once. Rest outside held stances where possible and extend recovery if movement quality or attention has not returned.

**Space and equipment:** Use one protected **10 m lane** for starts: start at 0 m, driving ends by 3 m, progressively stop by 9 m, final metre clear. One athlete at a time; close the lane during walking return and verify waiting/coach positions. The lane length does not establish individual stopping ability. E2 uses a modest selected distance inside a clear 3 m area with further empty space beyond. E3–E6 need separate clear stationary footprints; protect the entire bell path, landing areas and returns from crossing traffic. A wall is not confirmed equipment: verify that it is immovable, non-slip and clear, or use E3's floor replacement. KBs/DBs/benches are listed, but loads, dimensions, surface and quantities remain unknown. No movable box substitutes for a wall and no stacked plates are needed. The separate 12 m facility note remains unresolved; do not combine three lanes into a runway.

**Replacements — use instead of, never in addition:**

- **E1:** Use **Two-Point Standing Start instead of Falling Start** if the lean/recovery step is not controlled, keeping four starts and the same boundaries. This repeats an earlier family. If stopping space is insufficient, use one driving step at lower intent for the remaining attempts; stop the task if that still cannot be controlled. No extra trials.
- **E2:** Use **Parallel-Stance Broad Jump to Stick instead of staggered takeoff** if both legs cannot contribute without twisting: **1 × 4**, natural dip/arms, modest distance, 2 s hold and 20 s between reps. This repeats Class 3's family.
- **E3:** Use **Upright Single-Leg Pogo instead of Wall-Lean Pogo** if the wall or wall-pressure posture is unsuitable: same two hops/leg, 60 s between legs and a controlled two-foot reset. This repeats an earlier family. If same-leg reception is unsuitable, use **Bilateral Ankle Pogo instead**, **1 × 4** low hops; choose one replacement, not both.
- **E4:** Use **Split Squat Jump to Stick, same lead, instead of the scissor exchange** if switching disrupts reception: same two/starting lead and rests, no airborne leg swap. This explicitly repeats Class 2's task.
- **E5:** Use **Stationary Single-Leg High-Knee Run instead of Step-Over Run** if release causes reaching: same two cycles/target and rest, compact bent-knee recovery. This repeats Class 5's family at a smaller dose.
- **E6:** If swing competence, a suitable bell or clear bell path is unavailable, use **Paused Squat Jump to Stick instead of the dead-stop swing**, **2 × 2**, hands on hips, comfortable squat held 2 s without a re-dip, modest upward jump and 2 s bilateral landing hold. Rest **20 s between reps, 90 s between sets**. This repeats the earlier squat-jump fallback family and adds four bilateral landings in place of six nonflight swings.

**Quality rules:** Attempted/failed work counts as exposure. Adjust the next scheduled rep; repeated faults despite adjustment end the exercise. Pain, slipping, changed gait or lost implement/body control ends the affected task immediately. Record actual replacements, extra contacts, stopping steps, omitted work and reasons. No make-up reps or extra exercise slots. Incomplete delivery stays incomplete in the record.

## 3. Strength (Stabilization/Resilience) — Exactly 2 Exercises

Easy effort, approximately **RPE 3–4/10**. Retain these small strengthening doses without pre-fatiguing the loaded work.

| # | Exercise | Sets × reps | Specific job in this workout |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Short-Foot Drill** | **1 × 3 holds × 5 s per foot**, both feet supported. **5 s release between holds; 20 s between feet.** | Maintain heel and both forefoot bases as the working arch gently rises, supporting the foot repeatedly used for E1/E3. Keep toes long; reduce effort or use **seated foot doming instead of standing** for clawing/rolling. |
| 2 | **Side-Lying Hip Abduction** | **1 × 6 per side**, bodyweight; **2 s up / 1 s hold / 2 s down**. **20 s between sides.** | Give the lateral hip a small strengthening dose for holding pelvic position over one support leg as the other moves. Bottom knee bent, top leg aligned with torso, toes forward; reduce range if the pelvis rolls or the thigh drifts forward. |

Rest **45 s between exercises and 60 s after S2** before P1 preparation. Stop for pain or persistent compensation; do not add resistance to create a burn.

## 4. Strength (Primary) — Exactly 6 Exercises

Use challenging loads/leverage leaving approximately **2–3 technically sound repetitions in reserve (RIR)**. Keep Class 5's working doses and preparation rules. Actual prior loads are unknown: qualify today's load rather than assuming an increase or a previously completed set. No forced reps, maximal tests or automatic restoration of reduced volume.

| # | Exercise | Sets × reps | Specific job in this workout |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Split Squat — two dumbbells at sides** | **1 × 5 per leg**, 2–3 RIR; **2 s down**, strong controlled ascent. **60 s between legs.** | Retain loaded lead-leg extension from a stable base for the starting push and staggered projection. Both feet stay on the floor; modest whole-trunk inclination without rounding. Reduce load/depth for knee collapse, pelvic rotation or rear-leg hopping. The reduced single round limits overlap with starts and split-stance jumps. |
| 2 | **Romanian Deadlift — two dumbbells** | **1 × 6**, 2–3 RIR; **2 s down**, strong controlled ascent. | Retain hip-extension strength through a flexed-hip range, complementing E6’s brief rapid hinge with a controlled loaded range. Soft knees, bells close; stop depth before spine/pelvic compensation. Reduce range/load as needed. |
| 3 | **Seated Dumbbell Hip Flexion** | **1 × 6 per leg**, 2–3 RIR; **1 s lift / 1 s hold / 2 s lower**. **45 s between legs.** | Load thigh lifting separately from the light rapid exchanges. Secure a DB on the distal thigh above the knee with both hands; lift the knee a few centimetres without hand assistance or backward lean. Start on a fitted stable seat with foot supported and knee near a right angle. Reduce load/range for pinching, tipping or a shifting implement. |
| 4 | **Glute Bridge Walkout** | **1 × 3 complete cycles**, approximately 2–3 clean cycles in reserve. One cycle = **4 small alternating heel steps out + 4 back**, about **8–10 s**. | Strengthen knee-flexor support as the knee opens/returns, complementing E5's controlled foot return and the hip hinge. Keep the pelvis raised, knees soft at the far endpoint and return to the original heel positions. Shorten steps for sag/cramp; stop if control cannot be restored. This is capacity work, not high-speed swing simulation. |
| 5 | **Standing Dumbbell Calf Raise — bilateral, floor range** | **1 × 10**, 2–3 RIR; **1 s rise / 1 s top / 2 s lower**. | Retain near-straight-knee plantarflexion force for repeated upright support. DBs at sides, both forefeet loaded, heels return to floor. Reduce load for lost heel height, outward roll or bounce; do not lock the knees forcibly. |
| 6 | **Bent-Knee Soleus Raise — seated, bilateral DB loading** | **2 × 8**, 2–3 RIR; **1 s rise / 1 s top / 2 s lower / 1 s bottom**. **90 s between sets.** | Maintain ankle-force work with the knee bent, complementing P5 and soft-knee support during the drills. Secure weights on thighs above the knees; forefeet stay down and heel range stays repeatable. Reduce load for knee straightening, rolling or bounce. |

**Load-preparation sets, separate from working sets:** P1 **1 × 4/leg** bodyweight/light (30 s between sides, 60 s before work); P2 **1 × 5 easy then 1 × 3 moderate** (60 s between, 90 s before work); P3 **1 × 3/leg light** (30 s between, 45 s before work); P4 **1 short-lever cycle** (45 s before work); P5 **1 × 5 easy** (45 s before work); P6 **1 × 5 easy** (60 s before work). Additional small ramps, if needed, stay within the listed movement and are logged; no additional preparation sequence is invented.

**Between primary exercises:** **120 s after P1/P2; 90 s after P3/P4/P5**, before the next preparation set. Setup may occupy recovery; no extra required rest after final P6. If P5 balance limits productive loading, use **supported Single-Leg Calf Raise instead of bilateral P5**, **1 × 6/leg**, same tempo/RIR, 30 s between legs; preparation **1 × 3/leg easy**, 20 s between, 45 s before work. Verify stable hand support and log laterality. A fitted stable box may replace the bench for P3/P6.

**Timing and recovery:** Allow **72–82 minutes after Access & Prepare 1** with prompt individual equipment access: about 33 min explosive work, 5–6 min light strengthening and 33 min primary work, including teaching, rests, preparation sets and transitions. Extra instruction, ramps, queues or recovery can extend this. Existing preparation duration, booking, group and staffing are unknown; complete-session duration remains unresolved. A 60-minute complete booking cannot fit this version. Review actual sport, sprinting, other gym/classes and separate tumbling before scheduling. Nonconsecutive demanding lower-body exposures, often roughly 48–72 hours apart, are only a planning starting point; actual response and the full schedule govern.

**Progression note:** This class connects forward initiation, force from an offset base, rapid leg exchange and upright foot return through separate listed tasks; it is not a combined start-to-top-speed run. Four starts use the earlier two-step/3 m driving and 9 m stopping caps. Upright running is reduced to eight contacts, wall recoil to two/leg and dead-stop swings to six singles. All strength doses hold. No heavier load, greater lean/jump height or earned tolerance is inferred. Class 7 should revisit rapid hip extension and horizontal projection from stillness after reviewing actual responses; no later class is written now.

**Audit summary:** Exact 6/2/6 and original framework retained. Defaults: **4 starts; 4 staggered broad jumps; 4 wall-supported same-leg pogo landings; 4 split scissor-jump landings; 8 upright running contacts; 6 parked-single swings**. Jump/hop subtotal **12 events: 8 bilateral and 4 unilateral landings**, separate from running/slowing contacts. Primary work remains **7 rounds / 9 bouts / 54 dynamic reps plus 3 walkout cycles**. New variants have specific jobs; fallback recurrence is disclosed. See the [audit](../supporting/class_06_audit.md), [ledger](../progression_ledger.md) and [source/identity notes](../supporting/class_06_sources_and_exercises.md).

# Class 8 — source and exercise identity notes

**Reviewed 2026-09-13.** Local programming uses the requested Sprinting scope, ten-metre footprint and exact 6/2/6 architecture. OTA supplies coaching inspiration; these doses, geometry, alternatives and strength allocation are authored for this curriculum. No source validates the complete session or proves an athlete improved.

## Coaching sources and limits

| Source | Relevant contribution | Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| [OTA — Full Guide to Your 40 Yard Dash](https://blog.overtimeathletes.com/40-yard-dash-guide/) | Combines starts, acceleration mechanics and horizontal projection; includes a four-point origin within its kick-up drill and repeated unilateral jumping. | Class 8 uses a still four-point origin and only two small bilateral jumps per bout. The kick-up entry, triple unilateral bounds, longer run, weight-distribution percentages and handedness rules are not imported. No universal stance angles or performance guarantee. |
| [OTA — NFL Combine Prep Training](https://blog.overtimeathletes.com/maximize-your-speed-nfl-combine-prep-training-for-the-40-yard-dash/) | Explicit single-, double- and triple-switch wall variants, with attention to position and brief breaks. | Only paired switches are used; a comfortable verified lean, low count and full resets govern. A paired switch is a related rhythm constraint, not an unrelated new base exercise. |
| [OTA — Baseball Workout for Top Speed](https://blog.overtimeathletes.com/baseball-workout-for-top-speed-agility-and-hypertrophy/) | Butt-kick running with the thigh slightly forward gives a knee-fold recovery task distinct from higher-thigh and step-over drills. | Our eight-contact stationary version is gym support, not its traveling workout or top-speed running. No forced heel-to-butt contact, hypertrophy block, tempo running or agility work is copied. |
| [OTA — Ballistics Training for Athletes](https://blog.overtimeathletes.com/ballistics-training-for-athletes-how-to-build-total-body-explosiveness-power/) | Lists forward scoop and hip-hinge scoop throws among horizontal/hip-driven power choices. | Supports selecting the movement family, not four throws as a proven dose or a promised sprint improvement. No depth drop, catch, follow-up sprint or five-to-eight-set volume is imported. Containment and technically crisp release govern local intent. |

General supervised youth-loading and hip/ankle rationale remain documented in the [initial source register](sources_and_exercises.md). They do not validate this class or supply actual readiness data. A four-point-start research page returned a browser check on direct opening; its search excerpt is not used to claim a fully reviewed study, an optimal start or a collision-risk estimate for this setting.

## Local identity evidence

Inspected `docs/exercise-difficulty-review.csv` for crouch/four-point, repeated broad, split reception, double switch, butt-kick and scoop families. Relevant names/slugs exist for `repeated-broad-jump`, `medicine-ball-scoop-toss`, `med-ball-scoop-toss` and `standing-medicine-ball-scoop-toss`; name-only evidence does not resolve every variant.

Read the local generated forward-scoop assessment at `scripts/data/canonical-research/generated/scoop-toss-forward-rotational-identity/medicine-ball-scoop-toss.v1.json`. It explicitly defines a parallel, front-facing, two-hand underhand release after hip/knee loading, with no step, jump or catch and controlled retrieval. Its stored display name is **Forward Medicine Ball Scoop Toss**, slug **medicine-ball-scoop-toss**, variant **standing-two-hand-forward-free-flight-scoop-toss**. These are verified local record identifiers, not invented live application IDs. Its snapshot is a review artifact; publication/athlete availability was not checked.

The neighboring `countermovement-medicine-ball-scoop-toss.v1.json` identifies an unresolved direction/release label and a retired/archived source. Do not bind Class 8 to that ambiguous label or to the rotational scoop. Local evidence assertions and numeric difficulty values are not independent research validation and are not imported as athlete competence scores.

| Slot | Identity decision and relation to prior work |
|---|---|
| E1 Four-Point Crouch Start | **Proposed explicit addition:** no blocks, two hands grounded, still origin, rear foot/hands within 0–2 m and front toe at 1 m. Different hand-support/release condition from Class 3's one-hand start. No exact canonical record was found in the inspected CSV. |
| E2 Repeated Broad Jump | Use verified local name/slug `repeated-broad-jump`; **proposed explicit two-jump dose/finish variant** because no detailed generated definition was verified. Immediate first rebound differs from earlier held receivers. |
| E3 Broad Jump to Split-Stance Stick | **Proposed addition/receiver variant:** parallel takeoff, forward projection, modest split reception. The inverse of Class 6's offset-to-parallel task; no exact library binding claimed. |
| E4 Wall Drill Double Switch | **Proposed paired-switch variant** within the existing wall-switch family. Two exchanges occur without an intermediate hold; default history previously prescribed isolated switches. Same family is disclosed. |
| E5 Stationary Butt-Kick Run | **Proposed stationary variant** of an OTA-named running drill; eight contacts and one finish set-down. Knee folding with slight thigh lift differs from low dribble, high-thigh A-run and step-over release tasks; no exact local binding found. |
| E6 Forward Medicine Ball Scoop Toss | Verified forward local identity and variant above; our ball/target/rest/dose constraints are explicit modifiers. No default forward throw was prescribed in Classes 1–7. |
| S1/S2 and P1–P6 | Identities and working/preparation doses retained from Class 7; specific jobs rewritten for crouched push, reception, exchange and recovery. Actual load remains unknown. |

## History and practical qualifications

Default distinctions concern initial support, immediate force reuse, receiving stance, linked exchange, recovery pattern or implement release. A different name, cue or rep count alone receives no novelty credit. The double-switch and running drills remain related families. Every earlier default and contingency was considered; replacements deliberately repeat useful earlier tasks.

If E2 and E3 both need parallel isolated broad-jump replacements, E3 switches instead to the documented same-lead split jump, avoiding duplicate slots. E6's parked-swing and rapid-bridge alternatives are explicit recurrences. Replacements change exposure and comparison conditions and are never added to defaults.

Wall, start footprint, lane width, low-rebound ball behavior, floor rating, overhead clearance and group flow remain unconfirmed. A short target does not prove throw containment; use the non-throwing path when needed. All observed attendance, load, completion and recovery remain unknown. No exercise-library or application records were edited.

# Class 4 — sources, exercise identities and assumptions

Reviewed 2026-09-13. Sources inform particular choices; none validates this exact session, its youth dose or a guaranteed change in sprint speed. No long runways, published adult/elite volumes or additional preparation routines are imported.

## Evidence and coaching inspiration

- [Overtime Athletes: Sprint Mechanics for Maximum Speed](https://blog.overtimeathletes.com/sprint-mechanics-for-maximum-speed/) describes bent-knee recovery, straight-leg force drills and cycling. This supports the general combination of upright mechanics and targeted strength. Stationary A-run/scissor-bounce prescriptions are local adaptations; their small doses, contact rules and fallbacks are authored here. The article's preference for repeated drills yields to the user's explicit preference for unique drills, while mechanical continuity remains. Do not import outcome guarantees or aggressive reaching/pulling cues.
- [Overtime Athletes: Low Box Hip Switch](https://blog.overtimeathletes.com/use-low-box-hip-switch-to-sprint-faster/) describes keeping one foot on a small platform while the free foot touches the floor and returns, with pelvic control. Class 4 keeps that task but prescribes only three reps per leg with full resets. The platform is approximately 10 cm only if a suitable stable item exists; no assumption that the listed jump boxes include that height. Marketing claims about correcting imbalance or increasing speed are not treated as demonstrated outcomes.
- [Brooks et al.: Does restricting arm motion compromise short sprint running performance?](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35276457/) reports a small short-sprint performance difference with restricted arm motion and discusses compensatory upper-body rotation. This supports considering arm action in the posture task. It does not test seated arm drills or show that forcing faster arms improves sprint speed.
- [Weyand et al., 2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11053354/) and [Dorn, Schache and Pandy, 2012](https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/215/11/1944/10883/Muscular-strategy-shift-in-human-running) supply the previously reviewed ground-force and hip/ankle-function rationale. The specific jump, bridge, calf and hip-flexion choices remain programming inferences, not tested consequences of those studies. Stationary foot placement is not literal full-speed touchdown geometry.
- [NSCA youth resistance-training position statement](https://dxpprod.nsca.com/globalassets/about/position-statements/position_stand_youth_resistance_training---2009.pdf), previously reviewed, informs supervised, technically qualified resistance work. Age alone does not establish readiness and the statement does not certify this whole class or a fixed recovery interval.

## Local identity checks

Read `docs/exercise-difficulty-review.csv` for names/slugs and the generated straight-leg identity record. Slugs below are verified local lookup values, not invented IDs or claims that the live application publishes the exact prescribed version. No library/database content was changed.

| Slot | Lookup evidence | Binding and prescribed distinction |
|---|---|---|
| E1 stationary A-run | No exact matching high-knee/A-run identity found in the inspected CSV | **Proposed addition:** alternating airborne bent-knee exchanges, stationary, counted by foot contacts. It is not the prior A-skip or low-dribble record. |
| E2 single-leg vertical jump/stick | Related `single-leg-hop-to-stick` and `single-leg-hop-to-stick-low-amplitude` found | **Proposed explicit variant:** vertical countermovement, same-leg reception and terminal two-second stick. CSV names alone do not establish axis, amplitude or arm rules, so no exact canonical binding is claimed. |
| E3 straight-leg scissor bounce | Related `straight-leg-bound-march`; inspected `scripts/data/canonical-research/generated/straight-leg-bound-march.v1.json` | That record explicitly identifies unresolved march/bound conflation. **Proposed addition:** stationary, alternating, very low flight, softly extended knees, six contacts and terminal control. Do not bind a no-flight march or traveling bound to this prescription. |
| E4 low box hip switch | No exact matching low-box hip-switch identity in inspected CSV; official OTA description reviewed | **Proposed addition:** elevated support foot stays put; free foot taps floor and returns. Distinct from Class 3 step-up and from alternating box-foot jumps. |
| E5 arm action | `arm-action-drill` — Arm Action Drill — Seated or Standing; related `sprint-arm-action-switches` | Verified family name; selected seated bodyweight rapid-exchange variant with explicit count. Exact delivery dose/seat condition is authored, not claimed as a published database card. |
| E6 rapid single-leg bridge | `single-leg-glute-bridge` found; separate hold/isometric names also present | Verified dynamic family. Rapid-concentric, nonflight variant is an explicit local prescription; do not bind to a hold card or count it as the walkout. |
| S1/S2 and P1–P6 | Prior [source/exercise register](sources_and_exercises.md) | Retain the previous identity qualifications and DB variants. Names, tempo and preparation doses stay consistent; P1 working rounds reduce. No newly invented identifiers. |

Fallbacks are named in the class and history. Fast A-march and straight-leg quick steps explicitly remove flight; bilateral CMJ recurrence comes from the earlier optional family; the low-box fallback repeats Class 3's standing cycle. Standing arm action uses the same verified family with different support. Bilateral rapid bridge uses the verified glute-bridge family, but the rapid dose remains locally authored. Actual selected versions are unknown.

## Limits carried forward

No athlete attendance, load, recovery, actual ground contacts or class duration is observed. Bench/box fit, low-platform availability, DB ranges, surface, staffing and class size require on-site verification. The prescribed primary dose is challenging by technical reserve, not a universal weight. The 64–74 minute work allowance excludes the existing Access & Prepare 1 and unmodeled delays. Current user/spec seven-category and 6/2/6 requirements govern over the older facility template. No actual maximum-velocity exposure or transfer outcome is claimed.

# Vortex Athletics — 12-Class Focus Curriculum Specification

## Purpose

Develop a progressive, coach-usable **12-class curriculum for one requested performance focus area at a time**. Devote each iteration to the best defensible next class, not to filling twelve templates. Every exercise must have a specific role in the day's primary effort.

This is a workout-programming task, not a request to build software, redesign the exercise taxonomy, or create a weekly calendar. Use the exact framework and class structure below. Body control/tumbling is programmed separately.

"Best" means purposeful, appropriately demanding, feasible, and revisable against evidence and athlete response. Do not claim a workout is scientifically perfect or guarantee outcomes.

---

## 1. Exact performance framework

Preserve these **seven categories and their subcategories**. Do not add, merge, rename, or reorganize them without explicit instruction.

### Protracted running
- Endurance
- sustained pace
- pacing control

### Sprinting
- Acceleration (straight-line and multidirectional)
- Maximum velocity

### Jumps
- Vertical
- Horizontal
- Lateral
- Force absorption
- Elastic rebound

### Agility
- Deceleration
- Change of direction/reacceleration
- Reactive agility and anticipation

### Object control & receiving
- Tracking
- Catching/receiving
- Controlling/manipulating objects

### Upper-body force generation
- Pushing
- Pulling
- Straight-line projection (such as chest passes)

### Rotational explosiveness
- Upper-body emphasis (rotational throws, punches, and swings)
- Lower-body emphasis (rotational kicks)

Strength, stability, explosiveness, and resilience support the selected focus; they are not additional performance categories. Body control remains separate.

## 2. Curriculum scope and run behavior

A **focus area** is the requested training target within this framework. For example, "Vertical Jumps" maps to `Jumps > Vertical`. "Acceleration" maps to the complete listed subcategory, with straight-line and multidirectional applications available within that curriculum. A category-wide curriculum is appropriate only when requested.

- Each requested focus receives its own twelve-class progression. Do not treat twelve classes spread across all seven categories as twelve classes for each focus.
- Work on the requested focus only; do not generate every curriculum automatically.
- A class is an instructional/training exposure, not necessarily a consecutive day or one calendar week. "12-day workout for Vertical Jumps" means twelve numbered classes unless a calendar is explicitly requested.
- **Default run boundary: finalize one new class per run.** Review saved work, develop the next class, audit and revise it, save it and its handoff, then stop. The next run resumes from that state.
- If explicitly instructed to complete several classes in one execution, still finish, audit, and save each class before developing the next. Do not bulk-fill later classes or reduce their detail.
- Default target when this specification is invoked without another named focus: **Vertical Jumps**. Start at Class 1 only when no valid curriculum progress exists.

## 3. Fixed class architecture

Every class must use the following order and exact exercise counts.

| Section | Requirement | Intent |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Access & Prepare 1** | Reference the existing predetermined sequence. Do not create or modify it. | Existing preparation, supplied separately. |
| **2. Explosiveness** | **Exactly 6 exercises.** | Explosive practice supporting the day's primary effort. |
| **3. Strength (Stabilization/Resilience)** | **Exactly 2 exercises.** | Light-load, stabilization/resilience-focused strengthening supporting that effort. |
| **4. Strength (Primary)** | **Exactly 6 exercises.** | Challenging strength work most directly supporting that effort. |

There are **14 prescribed exercise entries outside the existing preparation sequence**. Do not add finishers, conditioning circuits, extra reaction blocks, accessory lists, or tumbling exercises. Non-exercise notes, assessment criteria, timing, and programming rationale may follow the four sections.

### Counting rules

- An exercise performed on both sides is one exercise entry; prescribe and account for work on both sides.
- Multiple sets of one exercise still count as one exercise.
- Load-preparation sets for an already listed strength exercise do not create another exercise slot. Identify them separately from working sets.
- An alternative or regression is a **replacement**, not additional work. State "use instead of," not "also perform."
- Do not conceal several exercises in one row under "circuit," "combo," or "series."
- Do not fill separate slots with the same exercise at slightly different loads or renamed duplicates.
- Related variants may occupy separate slots only when they have genuinely distinct jobs. For example, a paused jump and a countermovement jump can address different takeoff tasks.
- Do not count one performance of an exercise toward two sections. Avoid identical exercise prescriptions across sections merely to meet the count.
- Every prescribed slot must contain real, purposeful work. Zero-dose entries are not a way to satisfy the count.

## 4. Athlete and planning assumptions

### Baseline

Use **ages 12–14 with established basic lifting and landing technique** as the foundational prescription. Training history, readiness, technical competence, and available supervision determine suitability and loading; age alone does not.

Class 1 is the beginning of this curriculum, not necessarily the athlete's first training session. Do not automatically turn it into a beginner-only introduction or restart competent returning athletes at an unnecessarily basic level.

Keep the main output focused on this baseline. Include an exercise-specific regression or progression when needed for execution, but do not expand every class into multiple age-group programs unless requested.

### Known and unknown information

Read relevant repository instructions, current curriculum files, equipment information, exercise records, and athlete feedback when available. Use the user's current specification for this curriculum rather than silently importing an incompatible older session template. Flag unresolved conflicts with other governing requirements.

Do not claim an exercise, machine, lane length, class duration, staffing level, or athlete test result is available or confirmed unless the supplied context establishes it. Record practical assumptions. For equipment uncertainty, identify a suitable replacement rather than adding another exercise to the session.

Do not invent a duration for Access & Prepare 1. If its duration is unavailable, report the estimated time for the prescribed work separately and leave the complete session duration unresolved.

### Confirmed viable equipment and training space

The owner has confirmed the following resources are available for curriculum programming:

- 3 lanes, each 10 m long
- Barbells (child, teen, female, male bars)
- Rubber plates
- Dumbbells
- Kettlebells
- Sand bags
- Wall balls
- Slam balls
- Medicine balls
- Landmines (1 handed, 2 handed)
- Cones
- Small hurdles
- Agility ladders
- Battle ropes
- Boxes (for box jumps)
- Bands (light and heavy)
- Jump ropes
- Timing gates
- Force plates
- Pull-up bars
- Benches

**Programming constraints:** Use this inventory when selecting exercises and planning stations. Bodyweight exercises remain available. Treat unlisted equipment as unconfirmed, not automatically available. Apart from the three lanes and their 10 m length, equipment quantities, load ranges, dimensions, and device capabilities have not been specified; do not invent them.

The three 10 m lanes are not a confirmed continuous 30 m runway. Account for required run-up, stopping space, and throwing clearance without assuming extra space exists. Timing gates and force plates may support assessments within the listed exercises, using only capabilities verified for the available setup; do not add extra exercise slots to use them.

### Loading and execution

- Primary strength means challenging, technically controlled strengthening, not light balance work or a breathless conditioning circuit.
- Do not interpret "intense" as maximal testing, forced repetitions, technical failure, or maximal loading on all six exercises.
- Prescribe load selection through demonstrated ability and a clear effort target. The supplied example uses approximately **2–3 technically sound repetitions in reserve**, rather than a universal weight for every athlete.
- Stabilization/resilience exercises remain light and controlled. They should not become pre-fatigue tests that undermine primary lifting.
- Give each exercise suitable recovery, execution cues, and hold/regress/stop criteria. Use qualified supervision for the target cohort.
- Preparation sets for heavy working sets are allowed, but do not invent a replacement warm-up or an additional preparation exercise sequence.

## 5. Exercise-selection requirements

### One primary effort, complementary jobs

Before selecting exercises, write a short **daily stimulus brief**:

1. The specific performance result being trained today.
2. The key movement demand or limiting factor addressed.
3. The primary performance exercise or assessment anchor.
4. The distinct supporting jobs needed from the other exercises.
5. One observable quality marker and the day's important constraints.

Then choose exercises to fill those jobs. Do not choose fourteen favorite exercises first and invent generic benefits afterward.

### Explosiveness: six purposeful exercises

Identify a primary performance exercise where appropriate. Allocate volume according to importance; six exercises do not imply six equally large or equally demanding workouts.

Each exercise must involve an appropriate explosive intent or clearly relevant rapid force-expression task. Differentiate low-amplitude elastic work, maximal-height or distance efforts, approach efforts, unilateral work, and ballistic throws where relevant. Do not treat every repetition as equivalent loading.

Sequence the work so the key task can be performed with the required quality. Supporting drills must not exhaust the athlete before the primary objective. Prescribe full resets where appropriate and avoid turning maximum-intent work into conditioning through rushed recovery.

### Stabilization/resilience: two targeted exercises

Use light external resistance or suitable bodyweight strengthening to address relevant joint control, postural control, controlled force acceptance, or tissue-loading needs. Each must have a specific connection to the day's task.

These are strengthening exercises, not a generic mobility list. Do not default to an unrelated balance drill and abdominal drill on every day.

### Primary strength: six direct contributors

Choose the six exercises that most defensibly support the selected performance effort within the total workload. Assign each a specific strength role and justify overlap.

The first exercise(s) may receive the largest investment; supporting strength exercises may use fewer challenging sets. Six slots do not require equal volume or six maximal compound lifts.

Do not insert unrelated pushing, pulling, or other movements solely to create a generic full-body workout when the request is focus-specific. Do not confuse extra complexity, unstable surfaces, or fatigue with strength development.

### Exercise library and evidence

If an exercise library exists, use its canonical names and identifiers where available. Do not invent identifiers or claim an exercise exists in the library without checking. Label useful missing exercises as proposed additions rather than substituting an inferior choice merely because its name is convenient.

Distinguish the intended mechanical role of an exercise from a demonstrated performance outcome. Verify consequential claims with accessible primary research or official specialist guidance when tools permit. Keep a concise source/assumption record; never fabricate references or imply that sources validate the exact whole session.

## 6. Focus areas that need special care

Apply the same fixed structure to every requested focus without mislabeling exercises.

For example, sustained running is not an explosive exercise, and ordinary catching practice is not automatically strength training. For protracted running or object-control targets, this template may provide substantial **support training** without all the direct endurance or perceptual/skill practice needed for a complete performance program.

Build the strongest honest support session within the requested architecture. State any material direct-practice gap plainly. Do not quietly add a fifth training block, call steady running "explosiveness," claim general strength replaces catching skill, or claim the template fully develops a quality it does not directly train.

If the constraints cannot support a defensible session, explain the precise conflict and smallest proposed change. Do not silently change the exercise counts or pass an unresolved session as finalized.

## 7. Iterative development protocol

### A. Establish a small, provisional twelve-class map

On the first run, create a brief roadmap of **one or two lines per class**: intended emphasis, continuity from earlier work, and a likely progression or consolidation opportunity.

This map exists to prevent twelve unrelated workouts. It is not permission to prepopulate all twelve exercise tables. Do not lock in exercises, loads, or progressions before examining preceding classes. Do not force a three-phase or weekly structure unless it is justified for this focus and schedule.

### B. Before developing Class n

Read the saved curriculum brief, provisional map, preceding finalized class, relevant earlier anchor exercises, progression/workload ledger, unresolved issues, and any actual athlete feedback.

Explicitly distinguish:
- **Prescribed work:** what the curriculum documents say should occur.
- **Observed work:** what athletes actually completed and how they responded, only when reported.
- **Unknown response:** information that has not been supplied.

Never claim athletes improved, tolerated a dose, or earned a progression merely because the preceding class was written. Without execution feedback, create a conditional prescription and make its readiness assumptions visible.

### C. Design only the next class in full

1. Write the daily stimulus brief.
2. Define the jobs needed in the 6/2/6 slots.
3. Compare plausible choices for consequential slots and select complementary exercises.
4. Set working doses, loading, recovery, sequence, and quality criteria.
5. Account for total explosive exposure, bilateral/unilateral work, demanding strength work, and likely overlap with other training.
6. Estimate real execution time and delivery requirements.
7. Explain why this class is the appropriate next exposure, not simply a harder or more novel workout.

### D. Audit and revise Class n

Check counts, relevance, duplication, fatigue, technical demands, progression, load selection, recovery, equipment, group delivery, and timing. Revise the class before finalizing it. A polished table is not an audit.

Give particular attention to these questions:
- Does the primary task get sufficient high-quality practice?
- Does every supporting exercise earn its slot?
- Are several exercises loading the same tissues without enough distinct benefit?
- Do the two stabilization exercises leave the athlete ready for primary strength?
- Can all six primary strength exercises be performed productively after the explosive work?
- Are prescriptions clear enough for a coach to run without inventing missing details?

### E. Save, reassess, and hand off

Save the finalized class, then update the ledger and provisional map. Reassess the sequence in light of what was just prescribed and what remains unknown. Record the next class's intended job and conditional progression criteria, **not a prematurely completed next workout**.

At the next run, repeat the review before prescribing Class n+1. By default, stop the present run after this handoff.

## 8. Progression rules

Continuity matters more than novelty. Retain useful anchor exercises long enough for purposeful practice and comparison. An unchanged exercise is acceptable when its role remains useful.

For each recurring anchor, make the following traceable:

**Previous exposure → current prescription → reason for the decision → criterion for the next exposure.**

Possible decisions include maintaining the prescription, adjusting technique or intent, changing load or volume, altering range or execution demands, adding a relevant movement variation, consolidating, or reducing exposure.

Do not automatically increase every variable or make each class harder. Change only the variables justified by the objective and available response data. Regress, hold, or consolidate when appropriate.

Use advance/hold/regress conditions based on observable execution and readiness. Do not fabricate precise percentage targets or pretend different jump variants are directly comparable tests. Keep assessment conditions consistent when comparing an anchor.

Do not assume twelve classes must correspond to twelve consecutive weeks. Recovery and the athlete's full schedule remain separate programming considerations.

## 9. Workload, recovery, and delivery audit

Account for at least:

- Jump, hop, and bound repetitions; distinguish the intensity/type and single-leg versus two-leg demands.
- Throws, sprint repetitions/distances, and other ballistic efforts when applicable.
- Stabilization work and primary working sets, with per-side dosing made explicit.
- Effort targets, rest, equipment changes, and any relevant technical prerequisites.
- Other known sport, gym, and tumbling exposure. Do not insert separate body-control programming.

State counting conventions. Do not count `2 × 6 per leg` as only twelve total repetitions, equate all landing contacts, or label a workload "safe" solely because it fits an arbitrary numerical cap.

Estimate time using actual work, prescribed recovery, preparation sets, transitions, and group/equipment constraints—not a sum of active repetition time alone. Waiting in a rotation may supply recovery only when the actual athlete flow supports it. Do not double-count the same waiting period as separate rest.

If the required work does not fit an established session window, revise dose, equipment flow, or sequence while retaining meaningful work and the exact counts. Do not delete exercises, hide an overrun, or shorten necessary recovery merely to make the timetable appear feasible. Report an unresolved conflict explicitly.

Recovery guidance must be contextual. The example's suggested spacing is not a universal rule for every athlete, curriculum, or sports schedule.

## 10. Required class output

Keep the visible workout practical and close to the reference format below. Use normal Markdown tables with these four columns:

`# | Exercise | Sets × reps | Specific job in this workout`

Distance or duration may replace repetitions where appropriate. Include load/intent, key execution details, and exercise-specific rest in the row or immediately associated notes when the general section notes are insufficient.

Each class must include:

- Title: **[Focus Area] — Class n of 12**.
- Primary effort and foundational athlete assumption.
- A concise quality/performance marker, integrated into a listed exercise rather than added as a fifteenth exercise.
- The four ordered sections with exact 6/2/6 counts.
- Per-exercise dosage and a specific job, not generic "improves athleticism" descriptions.
- Recovery and loading instructions, with preparation sets distinguished from working sets.
- Relevant execution/stop criteria, practical timing, and scheduling notes.
- A short **Progression note**: what was retained/changed and why; what must be demonstrated before the next relevant progression.
- A short **Audit summary** with actual findings, adjustments, and unresolved assumptions.

Keep lengthy comparisons, evidence notes, and workload detail in supporting curriculum files when that makes the coach's class easier to use. Explain conclusions and decision rationales, not private internal deliberation.

## 11. Persistent state and resumption

Follow existing repository conventions when available. Otherwise use:

```text
docs/programming/focus_curricula/<focus_slug>/
  curriculum.md
  progression_ledger.md
  progress.json
  classes/
    class_01.md
    class_02.md
    ...
    class_12.md
```

**curriculum.md:** focus mapping, baseline assumptions, equipment/delivery constraints, provisional twelve-class map, relevant evidence/assumptions, and design changes.

**progression_ledger.md:** prescribed exposure totals by class, recurring exercise prescriptions, actual observations only when supplied, rationale for changes, and advance/hold/regress criteria. Keep prescribed and observed data separate.

**progress.json:** track the focus, target class count, last finalized class, next class, finalized file paths, unresolved issues, and exact resume instruction. A finalized document is not evidence that athletes completed that class.

**classes/class_nn.md:** complete coach-ready class with its progression and audit notes. Do not create placeholder class files and count them as finished.

On resumption, verify referenced files actually exist and reconcile inconsistent state before proceeding. Save files only in the current authorized working environment; do not claim writes succeeded without checking. Do not modify unrelated application code, database schemas, deployment settings, or existing exercise records unless explicitly requested.

After each run, provide the new class, saved-file locations, any material limitation, and a one-sentence handoff. Do not announce all twelve classes complete when only the map or a sample exists.

At Class 12, also audit the full sequence for continuity, coverage, realistic progression, and unaddressed assumptions. Correct substantive inconsistencies and document what changed.

---

## 12. Reference example — Vertical Jumps, Class 1

**Reference status:** The following is the user's supplied format and programming-intent example. It is not a locked exercise list, an independently validated prescription, or an instruction to reuse these exercises in every class. Audit and improve it when warranted while preserving the four sections and exact 6/2/6 structure. A production class must also include the timing, progression, and audit information required above.

# Vertical Jumps — Class 1

**Primary effort:** Improve vertical takeoff through forceful leg extension and coordinated arm action.

**Baseline:** Ages 12–14 with established lifting and landing technique. Loads should follow demonstrated ability, not age alone.

## 1. Access & Prepare 1

Complete your **existing predetermined sequence**.

## 2. Explosiveness — Exactly 6 Exercises

The **standing countermovement jump is the primary performance exercise**. The other five provide supporting practice; keep their volume modest rather than treating all six as full plyometric workouts.

| # | Exercise | Sets × reps | Specific job in this workout |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Low-amplitude pogo jumps** | 2 × 8 | Practice small, quick ankle-driven rebounds. Stay tall; prioritize rhythm and brief ground contact over height. |
| 2 | **Paused squat jumps** | 2 × 3 | Produce upward takeoff from a stationary position. Hold a comfortable quarter-to-half squat for 2 seconds; jump without dipping again. |
| 3 | **Standing countermovement jump with arm swing** | 3 × 3 | **Main maximum-height practice.** Coordinate the dip, leg drive, and arm swing. Record jump reach. |
| 4 | **Single-leg vertical jump to two-foot landing** | 1 × 3 per leg | Practice upward force production from each leg separately. Use a controlled height and hold the landing for 2 seconds. |
| 5 | **Two-step approach vertical jump** | 2 × 2 | Practice converting a controlled approach into upward movement through a two-foot takeoff. |
| 6 | **Light medicine-ball vertical scoop toss** | 2 × 3 | Practice rapid leg extension against a light external load. Launch upward and slightly forward into a clear throwing area; do not catch the return. |

**Execution:** Reset between individual jumps except pogos. Rest **60 seconds after pogo sets and 90–120 seconds after other sets**, extending recovery when needed. End the exercise when takeoff or landing quality deteriorates—do not chase fatigue.

## 3. Strength (Stabilization/Resilience) — Exactly 2 Exercises

**Light resistance, controlled positions, no grinding or burnout.**

| # | Exercise | Sets × reps | Specific job in this workout |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Low lateral step-down with a light dumbbell** | 2 × 5 per leg | Practice controlling the pelvis, knee, and foot while accepting weight on one leg. Lower for 3 seconds; lightly touch the free heel down. |
| 2 | **Light-band Pallof press in athletic stance** | 2 × 6 per side | Practice maintaining trunk and pelvic position against a sideways pull. Hold each press for 3 seconds without twisting. |

**Rest:** 30–45 seconds between sets. Finish feeling controlled, not exhausted.

## 4. Strength (Primary) — Exactly 6 Exercises

Use **challenging working loads**, leaving approximately **2–3 technically sound repetitions available**. Perform lighter preparation sets before the loaded compound lifts; the table lists working sets. Qualified supervision and technically controlled loading remain essential.

| # | Exercise | Sets × reps | Specific job in this workout |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Double-dumbbell front squat** | 3 × 6 | Main bilateral strength exercise: load the squat pattern and drive upward through both legs. |
| 2 | **Dumbbell Romanian deadlift** | 2 × 6 | Load the hip-hinge pattern with controlled lowering and forceful hip extension. |
| 3 | **Dumbbell split squat** | 2 × 6 per leg | Develop each leg's force contribution through a stable split stance. |
| 4 | **Loaded hip thrust** | 2 × 8 | Emphasize strong hip extension through the finish without arching the lower back. |
| 5 | **Loaded standing straight-knee calf raise** | 2 × 8 | Strengthen ankle push-off with the knees nearly straight. Use support so balance does not limit loading. |
| 6 | **Seated dumbbell bent-knee calf raise** | 2 × 10 | Strengthen ankle push-off with the knees bent. Pause at the bottom rather than bouncing. |

**Rest:** 2–3 minutes between compound-lift sets; 60–90 seconds between calf-raise sets. These are strength sets, **not a timed conditioning circuit**.

**Scheduling:** Treat this as a demanding lower-body day. The supplied example proposes approximately **48–72 hours before another comparably demanding lower-body session**, adjusted for recovery and including sport and tumbling loads in the assessment. Validate spacing against the actual athlete schedule rather than applying it mechanically.

---

## 13. Acceptance checklist

A class is not finalized until these checks have been addressed:

- [ ] Correct requested focus, mapped to the exact seven-category framework.
- [ ] Correct next class number; prior saved work reviewed.
- [ ] Existing Access & Prepare 1 referenced without being created or modified.
- [ ] Exactly six explosive exercise entries, two light-load stabilization/resilience entries, and six primary-strength entries.
- [ ] No hidden extra exercises, filler rows, or unapproved training sections.
- [ ] Clear daily objective, primary performance anchor where appropriate, and specific exercise jobs.
- [ ] Meaningful, differentiated exercise choices with a coherent order.
- [ ] Explicit working doses, loading intent, relevant cues, recovery, and quality criteria.
- [ ] Workload and per-side accounting reviewed; combined explosive and strength demands considered.
- [ ] Exercise equipment and station layout match the confirmed inventory; unconfirmed quantities, capabilities, and space requirements disclosed.
- [ ] Realistic delivery/timing assessed; unknowns and material conflicts disclosed.
- [ ] Progression justified without invented athlete outcomes or automatic escalation.
- [ ] Completed class and state files saved and verified, with a clear next-run instruction.

## 14. Example commands

**Start:**

> Follow VORTEX_12_CLASS_CURRICULUM_SPEC.md. Build a 12-class curriculum for Vertical Jumps. Establish the brief provisional map, then develop, audit, and save Class 1 only. Update the progression ledger and resume instruction.

**Continue:**

> Continue the Vertical Jumps curriculum using VORTEX_12_CLASS_CURRICULUM_SPEC.md. Review the saved state and prior prescriptions, develop and audit the next class only, and update all progression records. Do not assume prior prescribed classes were actually performed.

**Continue with observed feedback:**

> Continue the Vertical Jumps curriculum. Use these actual coaching observations to decide what to maintain, advance, or regress: [observations]. Develop and audit only the next class under VORTEX_12_CLASS_CURRICULUM_SPEC.md.

**Revise instead of advancing:**

> Review and improve Vertical Jumps Class [n] under VORTEX_12_CLASS_CURRICULUM_SPEC.md. Keep the exact 6/2/6 structure. Explain material changes, update its workload/progression records, and flag any downstream classes affected. Do not generate a new class in this run.

# Class 9 — design and audit

**2026-09-13. Previous goal turn: progress.** Class 8 and its shared records are saved; all checkpoint hashes match and state paths exist. The original specification matches its saved snapshot. Reviewed Classes 1–8, earlier upright/start and strength anchors, workload, all default/contingency identities, audits/source notes, equipment and feedback. No actual athlete results are supplied. Only Class 9 is finalized.

## Daily stimulus brief

1. **Result:** Maintain upright support while recovering a compact free leg and returning the foot near the hip.
2. **Demand:** Coordinate hip/knee folding, vertical force reuse, ankle recoil and controlled hip extension without drift or excessive trunk movement.
3. **Anchor:** Two six-contact bouts of stationary high-knee/butt-kick running. Observe the coupled fold, foot placement and upright position within these attempts.
4. **Supporting jobs:** Whole-leg vertical rebound; ankle-led recoil from a split base; a long-leg downstroke with the other foot planted; opposing arm/thigh timing with seated support; rapid unilateral hip return without a landing. Retained strengthening supports these same jobs.
5. **Constraints:** Existing Access & Prepare 1, exact 6/2/6, baseline ages 12–14 with established technique and qualified coaching, no top-speed runway, unknown actual response and no automatic escalation. New variants must earn their place beyond a different name.

## Selection and revisions

| Slot or issue | Decision and reason |
|---|---|
| Main recovery pattern | Use the coupled high-knee/butt-kick running pattern described by OTA, made stationary. Its explicit knee fold while the thigh rises differs from Class 8's modest-thigh butt-kick emphasis and Class 4's simpler bent-knee exchanges. These remain closely related running variants; if actual prior A-run technique already used this exact fold, record recurrence rather than claiming a new athlete experience. |
| Main dose | Reduce the initial idea of two eight-contact bouts to **two six-contact bouts**. Twelve contacts match the earlier upright-day allocation in Classes 4–5, without implying those sessions occurred. Two controlled finish set-downs are counted separately. No traveling sprint is appended. |
| Vertical rebound | Two small consecutive bilateral vertical jumps change Class 8's forward rebound direction to a vertical support task. Unlike ankle pogos, a comfortable knee/hip dip contributes. Reject depth drops, tuck jumps and maximal-height repeat jumps: their reception demands are not justified by feedback. |
| Split pogo | A small fixed offset distributes low ankle recoil through front/rear supports without the lead exchange or larger knee/hip dip of earlier split jumps. Use only **two hops per lead**, not four, to contain the additional ankle work. Stance alone is not advertised as a new physical capacity; its specific role is maintaining upright alignment through an asymmetric shared base. |
| Long-leg return | Use a stationary downstroke with the other foot continuously planted. Unlike Class 3's full recovery cycle or Class 4's scissor bounce, it isolates a low, softly extended-leg return with no flight. Reject aggressive pawing, high kicks and traveling bounds. The foot meets the floor near its standing position without scraping backward. |
| Seated limb timing | Synchronize each quick alternating thigh lift with opposing arms while the seat supports body mass. This adds limb coupling to Class 4's isolated seated arms and differs from wall-supported exchanges. It is one coordinated movement, not an arm drill followed by hip-flexion reps. The strength hip-flexion entry has a different loaded, hand-secured capacity job. |
| Unilateral hip return | A shallow bodyweight single-leg hinge ending in a rapid controlled rise gives hip-extension intent without more flight. Reduce the draft three reps/leg to **two/leg**, given overlap with the loaded RDL and walkout. No reach target, deep stretch, external load, catch or knee-drive combination. A stable light hand contact may help qualify the same hinge; floor-bridge replacements remove the standing balance task. |
| Strength allocation | Keep the eight strengthening identities, doses, preparation and rests from Class 8. P1 loads leg extension, P2 hip force, P3 thigh recovery, P4 knee-flexor capacity and P5/P6 ankle force with different knee positions. The single RDL working set and reduced split-squat/walkout doses remain; do not restore volume just because starts and throws are absent. |

## Workload and progression

| Entry | Default prescribed exposure |

| E1 | 12 upright running contacts, six/foot, plus two controlled free-foot finish set-downs, one/foot when bouts start on opposite supports. |
| E2 | Four bilateral vertical jump landings: two intermediate rebound receivers and two final held receivers. |
| E3 | Four bilateral split-pogo landings, two per lead configuration; each two-hop bout has one rebound receiver and one final hold. |
| E4 | Six fast nonflight target-foot returns, three/foot. The support foot stays planted. |
| E5 | Six coordinated knee/arm actions, three knee lifts per side, and six controlled foot returns. These are not six separate arm exercises plus six leg exercises. |
| E6 | Four rapid unilateral hinge returns, two/leg, and four gentle free-foot reset placements. No athlete flight or implement release. |

**Jump subtotal: eight bilateral landing events / 16 landing foot impacts.** Four are knee/hip-driven vertical jumps; four are low ankle-led split pogos. Their stress is not interchangeable. E1 running, E4 floor returns and controlled set-downs stay separate. No starts, start distance, wall exchanges/pulses, throws, swings or actual maximum-velocity runs are prescribed in the default path.

Class 8 prescribed eight bilateral jump receivers, eight running contacts, eight wall contacts and four throws. Class 9 changes direction/reception type and assigns twelve upright contacts, while removing starts, wall contacts and releases. More upright contacts within the new task is not an equal-load exchange, a global increase or a claim of tolerance. The earlier upright classes supply a planning reference only. Keep height, offset, range and tempo qualified today.

Light work remains **2 rounds / 4 bouts / 12 dynamic reps + 30 foot-seconds**. Primary remains **7 rounds / 9 bouts / 54 dynamic reps + 3 walkout cycles** (24 heel steps). Preparation remains **7 rounds / 9 bouts / 32 dynamic reps + 1 short-lever cycle** (eight heel steps). Actual loads, existing preparation exposure and outside work remain unknown.

Continuity is **Class 8 prescription → same Class 9 strengthening dose → retain directly relevant capacity while changing coordination demands → change only after actual technically clean work at target reserve and adequate subsequent recovery**. Primary uses 2–3 technical RIR; light work uses RPE 3–4. The bodyweight rapid hinge is a brief clean force-expression task, not another challenging strength set. If it becomes slow balance work, use the listed floor replacement.

Hold with missing feedback. With actual feedback, change only a demonstrated limiting demand; do not simultaneously increase running contacts, jump height and lifting load. Pain, slipping or lost control stops the affected task; repeated faults despite adjustment also end it. Failed/omitted work is recorded, never made up to reach a paper total.

## Replacement effects and duplication check

- E1 simpler A-run preserves 12 running contacts plus two finish set-downs and repeats Class 4. Its nonflight march version gives 12 returning-foot placements without the two extra running finish set-downs. Neither is recorded as the completed coupled default.

- E3 parallel bilateral pogo keeps four low landings but removes the offset, repeating Class 1's family. It stays mechanically distinct from E2's knee/hip-driven jumps even if both regress.
- E4 compact single-leg cycle-and-strike preserves six target-foot returns but changes the recovery path; explicit Class 3 recurrence. E5's no-seat option is six standing arm exchanges, feet grounded, with no knee lifts or foot returns; explicit Class 4 fallback family. This avoids duplicating E1's marching replacement in E5.
- E6 unilateral rapid bridge gives four hip rises, two/side, and removes four standing free-foot reset placements. Bilateral rapid bridge gives four rises with shared support. Both are disclosed Class 4 families and different from P4's knee-lever walkout. Record actual setup contacts and changed resistance/support.
- Supported unilateral P5 changes work to **10 bouts / 56 dynamic reps + 3 cycles**, preparation to **10 bouts / 33 reps + 1 cycle**, about one additional minute. Verify the support and log laterality.

# Class 8 — design and audit

**2026-09-13. Previous goal turn: progress.** Class 7 and updated records exist; all files covered by its checkpoint match their saved hashes. Reviewed the specification, Classes 1–7, relevant strength/start anchors, workload, all default/contingency identities, source notes, equipment and feedback. No athlete attendance, execution or recovery has been supplied. Finalize Class 8 only.

## Daily stimulus brief

1. **Result:** Release a stable crouched start into consecutive forward pushes, recovering the free leg without losing the support line.
2. **Demand:** Coordinate the change from two-hand support to alternating steps; accept and reapply force when the next contact follows without a long reset.
3. **Anchor:** Four four-point starts, observing hand release, first two steps and stopping within the protected lane. These scheduled attempts supply the quality record.
4. **Supporting jobs:** A small bilateral forward rebound; forward projection into a split receiver; two linked supported leg exchanges; rapid knee-fold recovery; hip-led forward implement release. Keep the eight strengthening roles and doses because they still serve these demands.
5. **Constraints:** Baseline ages 12–14 with established competence and qualified coaching; exact 6/2/6; existing Access & Prepare 1; ten-metre footprint; unknown actual response, wall/ball behavior and group clock. Prefer meaningful drill distinctions without inventing progress.

## Selection and revisions

| Decision | Finding and final choice |
|---|---|
| Start direction | No athlete-specific need for a lateral/backward start is established. Keep straight-line acceleration. A new facing purely for novelty would move attention toward turning/agility. |
| Four-point origin | Both hands support a still crouch before coordinated release; Class 3 used one grounded hand. This changes the support/release task, not merely its name. No blocks, fixed joint angles, handedness-based dominant-leg rule, kick-up rebound or forced head-down running are imported. |
| Starting footprint | Revise the default front-toe line to 1 m, with rear foot and hands fitted inside 0–2 m. Drive ends by 4 m and stopping by 9 m. This accounts for the body behind and ahead of the front toe without assuming space outside the lane. Use the same front-toe line for its standing replacement. Travel is bounded from that declared toe origin, not an exact centre-of-mass path. |
| Rebound choice | Choose two small consecutive bilateral broad jumps per bout, only two bouts. Unlike earlier isolated/paused broad jumps, the first receiver is used immediately for the next push. Reject triple single-leg bounds and external drops: they add reception demand without enough evidence for this cohort. The second jump is omitted if the first receiver cannot support it; no make-up attempts. |
| Split receiver | Parallel takeoff into a modest split landing changes Class 6's offset-to-parallel task and the earlier split-to-split jumps. It supplies a different acceptance demand after forward projection, with both feet sharing the receiver. It is not a simulation of a running foot strike. |
| Wall pairs | Two switches occur without the intermediate hold used in Class 2's isolated switches. The linked reversal, not changing a rep count, is the intended distinction. Four pairs provide eight contacts, not eight pairs. This remains a related wall-switch variant, not a new base exercise. |
| Knee recovery | Choose a brief stationary butt-kick run with a slightly forward thigh and heel folding beneath it. This emphasizes knee folding rather than the higher thigh lift of A-runs or the lower-leg opening of step-over runs. Reject an isolated prone curl as a less direct coordination task for today. No heel-to-butt target or forced trailing thigh. |
| Released hip drive | Forward Medicine Ball Scoop Toss supplies a hip-led external release without athlete flight, distinct from the retained/parked implement in Classes 6–7. Use a straight-ahead parallel stance, not an ambiguous rotational scoop label. Reduce the draft six throws to four and keep full retrieval/reset time. |
| Ball feasibility | A forward toss cannot be assumed to stop inside ten metres. Require a suitable light floor-rated low-rebound ball, a verified containment layout and modest target. If a fast controlled toss cannot remain contained, replace it with four parked swings; do not use an excessively heavy ball to force a short range. |
| Strength relevance | Keep the same S/P identities and doses. P1 loads leg extension/split reception, P2 the hip-led push, P3 thigh recovery, P4 knee-flexor capacity and P5/P6 ankle force at different knee positions. No generic upper-body lift is added because the ball passes through the hands. |

## Dosage, overlap and progression

- **E1:** Four starts, two/front-leg choice. At most eight driving strikes and 12 m of driving, contained within four × eight metres = **32 m maximum outward travel** from the 1 m front-toe origin to the 9 m stop line. Four stopping episodes; actual slowing/return contacts unknown.
- **E2:** Two bouts × two consecutive jumps = **four bilateral landings**, including two intermediate rebound receivers and two final held receivers.
- **E3:** Four bilateral takeoffs into **four split bilateral landings**, two with each leg forward. Total E2/E3 = **eight bilateral landing events / 16 landing foot impacts**. The split receiver and rebound receiver are different exposures despite the same foot count.
- **E4:** Four double-switch pairs = **eight supported foot contacts**, four/foot, plus **four controlled set-downs**, two/foot. E5 = **eight upright running contacts**, four/foot, plus **one controlled finish set-down**. Keep fast contacts, set-downs and jump landings separate. The audit added these deliberate set-downs explicitly rather than hiding them in incidental exit work.
- **E6:** **Four forward throws**, no prescribed athlete flight, catch or follow-up sprint. Ball ground contacts and walking retrieval are not jump repetitions. No swings or wall pulses in the default path. No actual maximum-velocity running.
- **Light work:** Two rounds / four bouts / 12 dynamic reps plus 30 foot-seconds. **Primary:** Seven rounds / nine bouts / 54 dynamic reps plus three walkout cycles (24 heel steps). **Preparation:** Seven rounds / nine bouts / 32 dynamic reps plus one short-lever cycle (eight heel steps). Loads and Access & Prepare 1 exposure remain unknown.

Class 7 also had four starts and eight bilateral jump receivers, but Class 8 introduces two immediate rebound receivers, eight wall contacts, eight upright contacts and four releases instead of pulses, controlled wall returns and six swings. It is a redistribution with different coordination/impact demands, not equal workload or evidence of improved tolerance. Limit jumps to modest distance, keep linked efforts brief and hold reduced primary volume. First scheduled attempts establish control; remaining attempts can be regressed or stopped.

Strength continuity is **Class 7 prescription → same Class 8 dose → maintain directly useful capacity without restoring volume → change only after actual clean work at target reserve and adequate subsequent recovery**. No load, distance or speed increase is earned from saved files. Use 2–3 technical RIR for primary work, RPE 3–4 for light work. If actual prior response remains unavailable, qualify today's entry demand and hold; unfavorable execution or symptoms require reduction/deferment.

## Replacement effects

- E1 standing retains the 1 m front-toe origin, four starts and the same drive/stop bounds. One-step versions used throughout cap driving strikes at four; actual path is still observed.
- E2 isolated broad jumps retain up to four bilateral landings but remove rebound receivers; this repeats Class 3's family. If a first landing fails, omitting its second jump reduces actual exposure rather than generating a replacement trial.
- E3 parallel reception retains four bilateral landings but removes the split receiver and repeats an earlier family. E2 and E3 replacements would otherwise become the same isolated broad jump: if both require replacement, use **four same-lead Split Squat Jumps to Stick in E3 instead**, as defined in the class. This is an explicit Class 2 recurrence with vertical projection.
- E4 isolated wall switches keep eight fast supported contacts but give eight controlled set-downs instead of four, because the lean is released after every switch. This repeats Class 2. Without a wall, high-plank isolated switches give eight fast extending-foot contacts, with the forward foot hovering and knees lowered for recovery; setup/knee placements are recorded separately. This repeats the earlier contingency with different support. Four pairs are not added afterward. Allow about one extra minute for repeated floor setup if needed.
- E5 nonflight heel-recovery march keeps eight target-leg cycles but replaces eight airborne running contacts with eight controlled foot placements; no equivalence claim.
- E6 parked swings give four floats instead of four throws, no athlete flight. If those are unsuitable, four rapid bilateral bridges supply nonflight hip drive with different loading. Both fallback families are disclosed in earlier history.
- Supported unilateral P5 yields **10 primary bouts / 56 dynamic reps + 3 cycles**, and **10 preparation bouts / 33 dynamic reps + 1 cycle**, about one additional minute. Other setup/range adjustments are recorded with actual identity and conditions.

## Timing and delivery

Individual prompt equipment access; teaching and work allowances estimated. Count teaching once if it takes place during recovery. Retrieval occurs before the toss recovery intervals, so it is not counted twice as passive rest.
